The most important recent development is the presence of contraception and equal rights. Suddenly, the drivers of human evolution have drastically changed. Now, people can wait for the right potential mates, rather than breeding immediately. And now a female's selection criteria is much more important. Effectively, many women are selecting men who have qualities that women deem would make them good fathers and husbands. So a lot of the changes may be in mentality.

A lot of scientists seem to be of the belief that human evolution has slowed/stalled. This doesn't make sense to me. I want to stress that while I am a scientist, I haven't performed any studies or published on this - this is just anecdotal / from my learning. Also, I am not passing any judgement, simply stating facts.

Evolution requires competition, and it selects for traits (phenotypes) that are favourable in the current environment. The thing is, our environment has changed massively in the last few hundred years. Firstly, mate selection has changed. As an example, 100 years ago, being fat was a desirable trait as (amongst other things) it was a show of affluence, child bearing capability, etc. Now we desire thin mates as they are healthier.

Secondly, there is considerably more gene flow between distinct populations (ethnicities) these days than 100 years ago. This is both because immigration has become so widespread, and because advances in travel technology have effectively made distant places so much closer.

Thirdly, advances in medicine and technology over the last 100-odd years have overcome many crippling disabilities and disorders. Offspring that once would have been non-viable are now surviving to sexual maturity. People with impairments that once would have put them at a disadvantage, now compete on a level playing field for mates. This, in particular, must be increasing our genetic diversity (making more alleles viable).

Finally, 100 years ago welfare was all but unheard of. Those without work relied on charity, their families, turned to crime, or starved. Many of these people didn't have the opportunity to have children (pass on their genetics). Those that did have children saw many of them not survive to sexual maturity (adulthood). Now (at least in socialist countries like Australia, where I live) the poor have a guarantee of a living wage even if they can't find work. Further, their children are raised, clothed, fed, and educated at the expense of the taxpayer, irrespective of how many children those families have. Further, families with a higher education (who tend to be better off) are now having less children than poorer families (amongst other reasons, women are leaving child bearing to later in life so as to establish careers). Consequently there is a massive shift in what traits are being selected for by the environment.

In summary, I think we are in for a period of rapid evolution. Many phenotypic traits emerge from a combination of genes (this is why classical eugenics didn't work). By supporting those who once couldn't have passed on their genes, we are now seeing more and more genetic combinations that never would have previously been possible. Just like mutations, many of these won't be positive, but there is the possibility of the emergence of new traits from amongst them. Effectively, humans are stuck in a local minima in our (evolution's) genetic optimization search. The above points are helping us overcome this. Additional to this (mainly due to the second point: immigration), I think we will see more homogenization of humans (less distinct boundaries between ethnicities).
